title: Can Charter Schools Survive Universal School Choice? https://fordhaminstitute.org/national/commentary/can-charter-schools-survive-universal-school-choice
author: Daniel Buck
summary: Daniel Buck examines a new AEI Conservative Education Reform Network survey of 285 charter school leaders across Arizona, Florida, and Utah, states with mature education savings account (ESA) programs, to assess whether the charter sector, widely regarded as the bipartisan education reform era's clearest success, can survive the spread of universal school choice. The survey data show charter schools are already losing enrollment to ESA-funded private alternatives, with nearly half of Arizona charter leaders reporting student withdrawals and 58 percent anticipating further enrollment declines, while leaders simultaneously report high compliance costs that ESA-funded providers do not bear. Buck's central argument is that charter leaders overwhelmingly want reform rather than abandonment of the public charter model, citing funding equity, reduced duplicative reporting, and streamlined special-education paperwork as their top asks, and that most surveyed leaders report the ESA option has had 'no effect' on their own interest in starting a private school, suggesting continued institutional loyalty to the charter model. He concludes that the underlying policy question, whether charters should be preserved through deregulation or allowed to face 'creative destruction' from ESAs, has a clear answer: charters offer distinctive strengths (serving special-needs students, providing accountability and public oversight, being tuition-free and scalable) that a market of ESAs alone would not replicate, and argues that if the sector declines it will be due to overregulation rather than any failure of the model itself.
points: The survey's headline finding, nearly half of Arizona charter leaders report students already withdrawing to use ESA funds, quantifies competitive pressure that was previously more anecdotal than documented.

Buck identifies the specific structural asymmetry driving the strain: charter schools operate under 'heavier compliance and resource constraints than traditional districts are' while competing against 'nimble, less-regulated ESA-funded providers,' a regulatory rather than an academic disadvantage.

Despite competitive pressure, the survey found most charter leaders report their state's ESA program has had 'no effect' on their own interest in starting a private alternative, evidence Buck reads as continued institutional preference for the public charter model over abandoning it.

Buck's policy prescription is specific rather than general: trim needless regulation, streamline authorization processes, lift enrollment caps, and address funding equity and duplicative reporting, framing deregulation, not new funding streams, as the primary lever available to preserve the sector.

He explicitly frames the stakes as a test of the broader bipartisan reform legacy: allowing the charter sector, 'one of the few reforms of that period that (just about) everyone agrees was a success,' to decline through overregulation would convert one of the era's clearest wins into 'just another failure.'
quotes: The charter sector remains one of the few reforms of that period that (just about) everyone agrees was a success. They're popular, they boast real academic advantages over traditional public schools, especially for poor kids, and, through competitive effects, they even improve the outcomes of students in those nearby traditional public schools.
Charter schools are now "forced to compete against nimble, less-regulated ESA-funded providers while operating under heavier compliance and resource constraints than traditional districts are.

In Arizona, where the universal ESA has been in place the longest, "nearly half of leaders indicated that students had already left their schools to use ESA funds," with reported withdrawals ranging from a single student to dozens or even hundreds in larger schools.

Most of them emphasized that they're more interested in reforming charter schools to allow them to better compete with ESAs than to abandon the market altogether, noting that charter schools maintain strong reputations and that they provide "appropriate governance, accountability, and oversight.

A strong education marketplace requires many options, public, private, and charter. Moreover, if the sector dies with a whimper, those within it suggest that it will come through overregulation, not its own failures.
To do otherwise is to risk letting one of the primary successes of the bipartisan education reform movement become just another failure.
